newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - The Europlug -- a symbolic EU failure.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - The Europlug -- a symbolic EU failure.

text.p: Europe's failure to agree on a standard power plug may seem a minor problem compared with monetary union and eastern enlargement, which top the European Union's agenda for the 21st century.

Yet the unsuccessful 20-year quest for a Europlug which can be used in sockets across western Europe has taken on a symbolic significance in the campaign to create a single market which makes life easier for the ordinary citizen.

When electrical standards body CENELEC announced the latest failure to agree last October, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel issued a critical statement, saying it must not be a model for the single currency.
After the "victory of national plugs" over the interests of consumers, Kinkel said, European citizens rightly asked:

"How are we Europeans going to realise a common foreign policy, the common European currency and the EU enlargement if Brussels can't even manage the harmonisation of six European electric plug norms?"
The proposal would have introduced a standard plug with two or three round pins to allow appliances to be used across Europe without adapters.
European consumers and producers of plugs and sockets play down the significance of agreeing such a harmonised system, arguing it may cost more than it is worth.
EUROPLUG WOULD BE "PUBLIC RELATIONS SUCCESS"

Different national plugs and sockets can create annoying and time consuming problems for travellers taking their hairdryers, shavers and computers across borders, especially between the continent and Britain or Ireland.
Advocates of a standardised plug say it would help implement the EU's priority goal of becoming closer to its citizens.

"The creation of a harmonised plug and socket system across Europe would be, if it were possible, an important political and public relations success," said CENELEC secretary general Stephen Marriott.
"There is a great deal of political pressure and pressure from some parts of the consumer movement and from manufacturers of appliances."

CENELEC (the European Committee for Electrotechnical Standards) was formed in 1973 to work out harmonised standards for electrical products to facilitate trade. It groups standards bodies from the 15 EU countries as well as Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

Despite the obvious advantages for consumers and manufacturers of electric appliances, CENELEC's national members have been unable to come anywhere close to a deal, largely because it would force them to change their present systems.
"It is a problem of commerce and cost and national habits," Marriott said, referring to opposition from several countries to the latest plug proposal.
"Their arguments were various -- partly cost, partly technical, partly economic, partly safety."
EUROPLUG MAY NOT BE WORTHWHILE
Despite the failure to agree, representatives of consumers and plug producers do not seem too concerned.

"I would suggest it is not as big an issue as it has been made out to be," said Bruce Farquhar, secretary general of ANEC, a group representing consumers on standardisation issues. "To a certain extent there is already quite a lot of standardisation."
For example, taking a computer to another EU country only requires a different plug when going across the Channel.
"How many people actually go across with stuff that needs to be plugged in? It is a small number," Farquhar said.
There could have been a solution, he said, but plug and socket manufacturers were content with the present situation.
"Quite a lot of people are happy with the way the market in Europe has carved itself up. It was an example of vested interests at work."
David Dossett, member of the management committee of the Coalition of European Plug and Socket Manufacturers, said there was not much demand for a common standard.

"It is not a standard that is required by the market place," he said. "The fact is that if you buy a washing machine in France or Germany or Belgium it is supplied with a plug which fits 85 percent of the sockets in continental Europe.
"What needs to be done is just to persuade those small areas which are left not using the standard to move towards the standard," Dossett said, referring for example to parts of Italy and Denmark.
EUROPLUG EFFORTS TO CONTINUE

Anxious that the Europlug failure should not overshadow other efforts, Marriott stressed "the enormous success" of harmonising other aspects of the electro-technical system, such as the generation and distribution of electricity.
"The problem is that the lack of harmonisation of plugs and sockets is a symbol and a very visible symbol," he said.
But the significance of a harmonised plug "in overall economic terms should not be exaggerated," Marriott said.
"I don't want the success of 99 percent of the tasks that we are faced with to be measured by the success or failure of a one percent problem," he added.

Marriott said agreement on a standardised plug was still possible at other levels. The dossier has been transferred to CENELEC's international counterpart, the Geneva-based International Electrotechnical Commission.
"They are working on it actively at the moment and we expect that a new draft will appear for voting at IEC level and in parallel at CENELEC level early in 1998," he said.
The European Commission, which has pushed hard for agreement on the Europlug, does not rule out legislative proposals on the issue even if this is unlikely now.
"It is not just a symbolic question," said a spokesman for EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann, arguing that there were real practical difficulties without the Europlug.
